video_title: The Story of Europe's Decline Isn't So Simple | Odd Lots
gist: Economist Dominik Leusder argues the Draghi-report 'Europe falling behind the US' narrative is largely a PPP/deflator measurement artifact and that Europe's richer economies are as productive per hour while choosing leisure, with US aggregate strength top-heavy and inflated by ~$1.8T of healthcare rents. The real European threat is the second China shock: Germany has lost over a million manufacturing jobs since 2021, and the EU's slow, divided response (Industrial Accelerator Act) risks too-little-too-late outcomes versus China's rapid retaliation.

themes.theme: Draghi gap is a measurement artifact

insights.claim: The widely cited claim that EU GDP fell from ~90% to ~70% of US levels (Jamie Dimon) is meaningless if computed at market exchange rates, because it mostly measures dollar fluctuations rather than real output.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: Headline 'Europe falling behind' narratives built on nominal USD GDP are FX artifacts; don't trade European decline on them.
insights.quote: all you're measuring is how the dollar has fluctuated over time

insights.claim: The Draghi report's centerpiece stat - EU GDP per hour in PPP terms falling from 90-something% to 70-85% of the US since 1995 - relies on constant-price PPP (2010 dollars) extrapolated with national-accounts real growth rates, which builds in a spurious downward trend.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: The 'robust stylized fact' underpinning EU competitiveness policy is methodologically fragile; current-price PPP snapshots don't show the same decline.
insights.quote: It's not it's not established by any sort of, solid economic data.

insights.claim: The US BEA applies hedonic quality adjustment to tech goods and services more aggressively than European statistical offices, lowering measured US inflation and raising US real growth by roughly 0.2-0.3 percentage points a year, compounding into a large artificial US-EU wedge.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: Part of the measured US productivity edge is statistical; cross-region real-growth comparisons in tech-heavy sectors overstate the US advantage.

insights.claim: There is no good measure to compare relative US-EU output trends over time; only current-price PPP level snapshots are defensible.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: Treat long-run relative-decline charts with skepticism; compare levels year by year instead.
insights.quote: we don't have a good measure to compare trends over time

insights.claim: On a current-price PPP GDP-per-hour snapshot the US is only slightly above the Western European aggregate and below Germany, the Low Countries and Nordics; excluding the top 10% of the income distribution, the US advantage disappears entirely.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: US aggregate strength is top-heavy - relevant to US consumer breadth and political economy.
insights.quote: if you actually then exclude, the, the top 10% of the income distribution, that advantage goes away entirely

insights.claim: The bottom half of the US distribution is significantly worse off than in any single Western European country except Portugal.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: Mass-market US consumer is weaker than aggregates imply; supports pricing-power/inequality-sensitive views on US consumption.

themes.theme: Leisure, consumption and US healthcare rents

insights.claim: Adjusting actual individual consumption (which includes in-kind public benefits like healthcare) for working hours makes US material well-being look 'pretty unremarkable' versus Europe.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: Welfare comparisons that ignore hours and in-kind benefits overstate US superiority.

insights.claim: The US spends about 50% more per person on healthcare than its consumption level predicts relative to other advanced countries - roughly $1.7-1.9 trillion a year in excess spending - driven by prices per unit of care rather than utilization.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: US healthcare is a ~$1.8T annual rent pool; policy targeting prices is a large latent risk for hospitals, insurers and middlemen.

insights.claim: High US prices in non-tradable sectors like healthcare, legal services and education reflect rent seeking by hospitals, insurers, trade associations and middlemen rather than a Balassa-Samuelson-style productivity spillover, so PPP adjustment is not 'hiding' US strength.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: Rents concentrate income in the top 10-20% while imposing costs on the rest - a political vulnerability for healthcare intermediaries.
insights.quote: that assumes that these prices are not a function of, of, of rent seeking, which unfortunately, I think the preponderance of the evidence shows they are

insights.claim: Europe's richer economies (Central Europe, Low Countries, Nordics) genuinely work far fewer hours while maintaining similar employment rates; evidence suggests a substitution effect where productivity reduces hours and lower hours raise productivity, not a labor market dysfunction. Informal hours in Spain and Italy don't change this much.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: Lower European hours are a preference, not a failure signal; don't read hours gaps as structural weakness.
insights.quote: they do work much, much less

insights.claim: Europe's real problem is weak performance in its own terms over 10-15 years due to poor macro policy choices (which the US does well), plus internal divergence such as Italy's South declining in absolute terms during a 20-year stagnation unique in the G7.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: The bear case on Europe is macro-policy and regional, not relative-tech; fiscal/macro regime shifts are the lever to watch.

insights.claim: Tracy Alloway argues that if you are bullish on AI-driven productivity diffusion you should be bullish on Europe, since no region is more motivated to raise output per hour so it can keep its leisure.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: AI adoption by European incumbents could be a margin story; watch labor-cost cuts like BMW's.
insights.quote: if you are bullish on AI and its ability to boost productivity across the board, in my mind you have to be bullish on Europe

themes.theme: Europe and AI: adopt, don't build frontier

insights.claim: Europe will not build a frontier AI model any time soon and shouldn't try; it should focus on tech-stack sovereignty from the US and China and on what fits corporate needs, where near-frontier models like Mistral suffice.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: European AI value accrues to adopters and sovereign-stack providers, not frontier-model builders.

insights.claim: Mistral is launching models built on Chinese model weights because it lacks the compute to train its own, creating a new dependency issue for European AI sovereignty.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: European 'sovereign AI' still depends on Chinese open weights and foreign compute - a gap for European compute/datacenter buildout.

insights.claim: As with prior tech waves, European consumers will likely capture AI's welfare gains via lower prices even though US firms innovate and hold legally entrenched moats in Europe.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: US AI vendors keep European revenue; European corporates get the productivity surplus.

insights.claim: BMW is targeting shedding a fifth of its manager roles with the help of AI, per a headline during recording; hosts question whether trimming management layers can make European automakers competitive with Chinese rivals.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Early concrete case of AI-driven white-collar cost cuts at a European industrial; cost cuts may not close the China gap.

themes.theme: Second China shock hits German industry

insights.claim: Germany has shed over a million manufacturing jobs since 2021, coinciding with China's industrial-policy shift and the energy crisis, in what looks like a disorderly decline in industrial employment.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: German industrials face structural, not cyclical, pressure; supports underweighting exposed German manufacturing.
insights.quote: Germany alone has shed over a million jobs in the manufacturing sector since 2021

insights.claim: The first China shock benefited Germany as a supplier of high-tech goods to China; it has flipped as China moved up the value chain while keeping lower-end manufacturing, aided by IP transfer that is greatest from Germany.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: German exporters' China franchise is eroding into direct competition in third markets.

insights.claim: German chemical employment has fallen the least among big sectors despite the highest exposure to energy and Chinese competition, because of labor hoarding amid skilled-labor shortages, so employment data understates the shock; Chinese chemical export volumes are sharply up while German ones are down.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: Employment masks the damage at German chemicals (e.g., margin/volume losses); expect lagged layoffs or restructuring.

insights.claim: China, after its housing bubble burst, intensified manufacturing subsidies amid weak domestic demand and export price deflation; per Brad Setser's work, more than half of China's GDP growth may depend on net exports.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: China's export dependence makes Europe - the only big open market - the pressure valve for overcapacity.

insights.claim: China is resisting yuan appreciation, adding to imbalances alongside industrial policy, and Europeans are too slow to address the currency dimension.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: An undervalued CNY sustains export pressure; watch for EU currency-related trade measures.

insights.claim: Far-right parties are performing strongly in German regional elections by framing industrial decline as incumbent, green and energy policy failure, though evidence suggests it is mostly driven by the external China trade shock.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: Industrial decline is translating into political risk in Germany, raising odds of policy shifts on energy and trade.

insights.claim: European energy policy is 'appalling' and has significantly damaged German industrial prospects.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: Energy costs remain a structural headwind for European energy-intensive industry.

themes.theme: EU trade response: slow, divided, retaliation risk

insights.claim: The EU's core response to Chinese trade, the Industrial Accelerator Act with buy-European provisions effectively aimed at China and protecting the auto market, is in review and might be implemented only mid next year, slowed by France-Germany splits and union disagreements.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: EU protection for autos arrives slowly and diluted; don't front-run a strong tariff wall for European automakers.

insights.claim: China's complaint to the European Commission over the Industrial Accelerator Act argued its capacity utilization is normal for a growing economy, an implicit concession that its domestic imbalances are real.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: Signals Beijing recognizes the overcapacity critique, possibly opening room for negotiated concessions.

insights.claim: The EU-China Trade and Investment Consultation Mechanism has yielded little beyond vague rare-earth assurances, with an early-October meeting in Beijing pending.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: Low expectations for near-term EU-China trade deals; rare-earth supply assurances remain soft.

insights.claim: Chinese retaliation is institutionalized and rapid: after the EU sanctioned some Chinese entities in late July for supporting Russia's war effort, China placed major European industrial firms on its own entity list the next day; the EU lacks equivalent capacity.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: European industrials with China exposure carry asymmetric retaliation risk to any EU trade move.

insights.claim: Base case: the EU acts next year with too little, China responds with a concession because it depends on the EU market, the EU accepts it for lack of internal consensus, and the industrial shift continues; worst case is a full-blown trade war. Escalation willingness may outrun resilience to Chinese retaliation.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: Expect continued erosion for European industry with tail risk of trade war; position for slow-burn decline rather than a policy rescue.
insights.quote: the worst scenario is a full blown trade war

insights.claim: EU policymaking suffers a 'joint decision trap' - domestic coalitions plus 27 states with veto points - yielding too-little-too-late, lowest-common-denominator responses.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: Discount the speed and force of any EU industrial or trade policy announcement.

insights.claim: Europeans were slow on China partly because evidence of China's mercantilist turn was politically tainted by association with Trump, and because, per Adam Tooze, Europeans are the 'Taliban of neoliberalism' on trade; Brad Setser and others pushed German consensus over the past 18 months.
insights.speaker: Dominik Leusder
insights.so_what: The policy Overton window on China has shifted decisively toward protectionism on both sides of the Atlantic.
